summary: Extends the URL MIME External-Body access type so any MIME part of a SIP message can be referred to indirectly by a URI. This meets the content indirection requirements of SIP. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Instead of stuffing a big photo into a note, you write down where the photo can be found and let the reader fetch it.

questions: mime part referenced by uri in sip
how does sip reject content indirection
subtitle: How a SIP message can point to a body part by URI instead of carrying it, using the message/external-body type.

tldr.problem: SIP is not a general data transport, and large or remote content can overload proxies, strain slow links or live somewhere other than on the endpoint.
tldr.mechanism: A SIP body part is replaced by a message/external-body part that names a URI, with parameters for expiry, size and hash and headers for type, purpose and version. The receiver fetches the content over HTTP or another protocol.
tldr.outcome: Any MIME part of a SIP message can be sent indirectly, and the receiver can decide whether to fetch it. Security relies on screening URIs, S/MIME and an optional SHA-1 hash.

today: RFC 4483 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 2017 and RFC 3261.

sections.title: Why Indirect Content
sections.content:
RFC 4483 defines content indirection for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). SIP messages have a start line, headers and an optional body, but unlike HTTP, SIP is not designed as a general-purpose data transport protocol.

Indirection helps in several cases. On bandwidth-limited links, the recipient can use metadata to decide whether to fetch the content. Large content can overload intermediate proxies, so it is moved out of the signaling network. And the data may not reside on the endpoint at all. The receiver then retrieves it by a non-SIP channel such as HTTP, FTP or LDAP.

The mechanism only changes transport. Apart from that, an indirect body part is equivalent to an in-line one and gets the same treatment. The RFC builds on the URL access type of RFC 2017, which extends message/external-body from RFC 2046. An earlier approach with the text/uri-list type could not carry per-URI attributes.
sections.eli5: If a package is too big for the mailbox, you leave a note saying where to pick it up. The note counts the same as the package.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples. In presence notification, a presence document may be larger than the recommended size for a SIP NOTIFY request, especially if it combines information from several endpoints. The server sends a NOTIFY with a URI, and the watcher fetches the document with an HTTP GET.

In document sharing, one party in an instant messaging conversation sends a MESSAGE request with a pointer to a document. Carrying the document itself is not an appropriate use of the signaling channel, and it may sit on an unrelated server. The recipient fetches it with HTTP GET.
sections.eli5: A long report is posted on a website and you only text the link, so the chat stays quick.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.content: The RFC lists what any solution MUST provide. It must be possible to give the location by URI, and to give the length, the type and the disposition of each URI independently. It must be possible to label the content so a receiver can tell if it changed, to give a time span for which the URI is valid, and for both sides to indicate support, with a fallback if one side cannot. Parties must be able to negotiate the content type and the URI scheme, and processing must need no human intervention. Integrity and confidentiality of the URI SHOULD be possible. Finally, it must work for any SIP message that could otherwise carry the content as a body.
sections.eli5: The note has to say where, how big, what kind, how long the link works and whether the thing changed, and both sides must agree they understand notes.

sections.title: Declaring Support and Rejecting
sections.content:
A user agent shows it supports indirection by listing message/external-body in its Accept header, optionally along with other types it accepts directly or indirectly. Agents that support indirection MUST support it for application/sdp, and MUST support receiving an HTTP URI. Other URI schemes MAY be used.

A UAS that cannot or does not wish to support indirection MUST reject the request with a 415 Unsupported Media Type response. The UAC can read the Accept header in that response: if message/external-body is missing, indirection is not supported, and if the specific media type is missing, that type is not supported.

Indirect content can be marked optional using the Critical-Content mechanism of RFC 3459. If the UAS cannot fetch or render an optional part, it MUST NOT return an error.
sections.eli5: Before sending a note, you tell the other side you can read notes. If they cannot, they answer that they do not understand, and you send the thing itself.

sections.title: Describing the URI and the Content
sections.content:
The URI goes in a URL parameter of the message/external-body Content-Type, with access-type="URL". Other details use further parameters and entity headers:

  • expiration is mandatory. It is an RFC 1123 date-time in GMT, and it can span minutes to years.
  • size in bytes SHOULD be given when known. A UAS may answer with a 513 error if the size is too large.
  • hash is a hexadecimal SHA-1 hash that the sender includes if it knows the content and wants the receiver to validate it.
  • Content-ID labels the content. A change in content MUST change the Content-ID, and repeated messages about the same content SHOULD reuse it so receivers can cache.
  • Content-Type of the content SHOULD be present, and may be omitted if the URI scheme can negotiate its own type.
  • Content-Disposition MUST be present for all indirect content.
  • Content-Description MAY hold free text for the user, but MUST NOT be used to decide how to handle the body.

Several URIs go in a multipart MIME body, with each URI in its own entity, and indirect parts may be mixed with in-line parts. The existing SIP headers Call-Info, Error-Info and Alert-Info MUST be used in preference to this mechanism where they apply.
sections.eli5: The note carries the address, an expiry date, the size and a fingerprint so you can check that the thing you got is the right one.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content: The RFC shows a single indirection in an INVITE, where the body is an application/sdp part fetched from an HTTP URL with size=231. It also shows a MESSAGE with a multipart/mixed body holding two image/png parts, each referenced by its own URL and size, each with a Content-ID, a disposition of render and a description.
sections.eli5: A message can hold several notes, one for each picture, and each note says where its picture lives.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Indirection adds risk. The RFC names these abuses: choosing a weaker protocol for the transfer, making the recipient spend resources (an active FTP URL uses 2 connections per message), port scanning by pointing at internal resources, and leaking sensitive details such as an internal user name or location in the URL. Careful screening of URIs both received and sent can mitigate all of these.

The mechanism relies on RFC 3261 and S/MIME for confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the URI. Securing the transfer itself is up to the underlying protocol. With HTTP, applications SHOULD support HTTPS and MUST support upgrading to TLS with starttls. Trust is not transitive, so a UAS SHOULD NOT trust the object just because it trusts the sender of the URI.

If the UAC knows the content in advance it SHOULD include the hash, and the recipient MUST check it and report any mismatch to the user. When a hash is present, the UAS MUST ignore certificate validation results and compare the hash instead. Without a hash, the sender SHOULD use schemes with message integrity such as https, and the UAS MUST verify server certificates against its trusted authorities.
sections.eli5: A note could send you to a bad place, so you check the address, and a fingerprint tells you whether you got the right thing.
